<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting
Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Center for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (CAIRO)Technical University of Applied Sciences Würzburg-Schweinfurt (THWS),Würzburg, Germany
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Real-world personally identifiable information (PII) redaction often
operates on document images—scans, screenshots, and PDF
renderings—where OCR errors, layout structure, and visual noise
determine whether sensitive information is actually removed. Existing
PII benchmarks are mostly text-centric and do not measure
document-level redaction risk: a page remains unsafe if even one
identifier is missed. We introduce LeakageBench, a challenge set of
500 document images with 11,954 GDPR-aligned PII annotations spanning
direct identifiers, linkage keys, and contextual re-identification
surfaces. We evaluate generic OCR pipelines, commercial and
task-adapted OCR-dependent detectors, and OCR-free vision-language
models using entity-level F1, group-wise leakage, and document-level
leakage metrics. Code Interpreter raises GPT-5.5 localization F1 from
0.090 to 0.249, but critical page-level leakage remains 0.968. These
results show that stronger detection and tool assistance improve
localization without making most pages safe for release. LeakageBench
provides a diagnostic benchmark for high-recall, spatially grounded
PII redaction in document images.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_align_bottom">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center" style="width:345.0pt;"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"></span></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Organizations routinely redact personally identifiable information
(PII) from scanned and rendered business documents. OCR errors,
complex layouts, repeated identifiers, and visual noise make this more than a clean-text tagging problem. Most PII benchmarks measure
span-level precision, recall, and F1 on text, while document-understanding benchmarks typically target selected key fields. Neither directly measures release safety: a page remains unsafe when any in-scope identifier remains visible. Evaluation must therefore capture both entity-level localization quality and residual page-level leakage.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Redaction presents an asymmetric operational trade-off. False
positives unnecessarily obscure useful document content, whereas a
single false negative can make a page unsafe to release. We therefore
treat document-level leakage as a recall-oriented complement to, rather than a replacement for, localization and typing F1, which also penalize over-redaction through unmatched predictions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LeakageBench</span>, a challenge set of <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">500</span>
document-page images containing <span id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">11,954</span> localized PII
annotations. Its GDPR-aligned schema distinguishes <em id="S1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">direct identifiers</em>, <em id="S1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">linkage keys</em>, and <em id="S1.p3.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">contextual re-identification surfaces</em>. Using a shared image-space interface,
LeakageBench exposes a stark deployment gap: even the strongest evaluated configuration leaks critical Direct+Linkage PII on 96.8% of applicable pages. Our diagnostics attribute these failures to
schema coverage, OCR recoverability, detection, interface validity, and spatial grounding.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our contributions are: (1) a controlled, densely annotated document-image redaction challenge set; (2) a privacy-oriented schema covering direct, linkage, and contextual identifiers; (3) release-oriented document-level leakage metrics reported alongside entity-level F1; and (4) a unified diagnostic evaluation identifying why OCR-dependent and OCR-free systems continue to leak PII.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Text-based PII detection and anonymization.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Text-based benchmarks cover legal documents, regulatory categories,
student writing, and clinical narratives
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pilán et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gambarelli et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mo et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Holmes et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stubbs et al., 2015</a>)</cite>.
They establish methods for span-level PII detection and anonymization,
but exclude document-image artifacts, spatial localization, and
page-level release safety.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Document-image understanding.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FUNSD, SROIE, CORD, and DocVQA evaluate form understanding, receipt
extraction, OCR, and visually grounded question answering
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jaume et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mathew et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.
BuDDIE broadens coverage to multiple business-document tasks and
includes person- and address-related fields
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. However, these benchmarks target
task-specific extraction rather than exhaustive PII localization and
residual redaction leakage.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">OCR-based and OCR-free document models.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">OCR-based models such as LayoutLM and LayoutLMv3 combine recognized text with two-dimensional layout
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, whereas OCR-free models such as Donut generate structured outputs directly from document images <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. For redaction, the former can propagate OCR and text-to-box alignment errors, while the latter must jointly learn visual reading and spatial localization. LeakageBench evaluates both through a common image-space prediction interface.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Leakage-oriented privacy evaluation.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">PRvL evaluates LLM-based PII redaction and residual exposure
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Garza et al., 2025</a>)</cite>; ProPILE studies
privacy leakage through targeted probing
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2023</a>)</cite>; and RedactBuster shows that redacted documents can remain vulnerable to downstream inference
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beltrame et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
These works motivate exposure-oriented evaluation, but do not provide a localized document-image benchmark with a page-level release criterion.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Task and Evaluation Protocol</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Task definition</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate <em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">PII redaction on document images</em>.
Given a page image—a scan, screenshot, or PDF rendering—a system must identify every visible region containing personally identifiable information, assign each region a schema type, and optionally extract its text value. Each gold instance is represented by an image-space bounding box, a fine-grained PII type, a risk group, and an optional verbatim value string.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The task is redaction-oriented rather than text-only: predictions must be spatially grounded so that the sensitive region can be masked on the image. This makes recall the primary safety concern. A page remains unsafe if even one in-scope identifier is missed, regardless of average entity-level performance. Inference is page-local: each rendered page is processed independently, and prediction–gold matching is performed only within that page. No cross-page context is provided. Accordingly, DocLeak is computed over document pages; evaluating multi-page contextual inference remains future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Prediction format</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A system outputs a set of predicted instances</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}=\{(\hat{b}_{j},\hat{t}_{j},\hat{v}_{j},\hat{s}_{j})\}_{j=1}^{M}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>b</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>t</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}=\{(\hat{b}_{j},\hat{t}_{j},\hat{v}_{j},\hat{s}_{j})\}_{j=1}^{M},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{b}_{j}=(x_{\min},y_{\min},x_{\max},y_{\max})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>b</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{b}_{j}=(x_{\min},y_{\min},x_{\max},y_{\max})</annotation></semantics></math> is an axis-aligned bounding box in pixels, <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{t}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>t</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{t}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> is a PII type, <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{v}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{v}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> is an optional extracted value string, and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{s}_{j}\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{s}_{j}\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> is an optional confidence score.
This unified interface supports both OCR-assisted pipelines, where boxes and values are derived from OCR spans, and OCR-free vision-language models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Instance matching</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We score predictions using one-to-one matching within each page. A predicted
box <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>b</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{b}</annotation></semantics></math> is eligible to match a ground-truth box <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> when
<math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{IoU}(\hat{b},b)\geq\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>IoU</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>b</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{IoU}(\hat{b},b)\geq\tau</annotation></semantics></math>. We enumerate all eligible pairs and
greedily select them in descending IoU order, ensuring that each prediction and
ground-truth instance is used at most once. A selected pair counts as a
localization match regardless of type and as a typed match only when the
predicted and ground-truth PII types agree. When values are available, value
correctness is evaluated only for matched pairs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Headline DocLeak uses type-aware matching: a gold instance is counted
as protected only when an IoU-eligible prediction has the same PII
type. This conservative criterion is used in
Tables <a href="#S6.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 6 Results ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>–<a href="#S6.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 6 Results ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. Diagnostic
attribution additionally uses type-agnostic matching because a wrongly
typed but correctly localized box would still mask the identifier.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Metrics</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report entity-level F1 and document-level leakage. The former measures
average detection quality; the latter measures whether any PII remains
unmatched on a page.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Entity-level performance.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{F1}_{\mathrm{loc}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F1</mi><mi>loc</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{F1}_{\mathrm{loc}}</annotation></semantics></math> is page-macro localization F1 using
type-agnostic matching. <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{F1}_{\mathrm{type}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F1</mi><mi>type</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{F1}_{\mathrm{type}}</annotation></semantics></math> requires both
<math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{IoU}\geq\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>IoU</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{IoU}\geq\tau</annotation></semantics></math> and the correct PII type, and is macro-averaged
over ground-truth types. Unless stated otherwise, <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.75" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.75</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Document-level leakage.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A page leaks if at least one in-scope ground-truth instance is unmatched:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{DocLeak}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}}\mathbb{1}[d\text{ leaks}]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>DocLeak</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><mn>𝟙</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext> leaks</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{DocLeak}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}}\mathbb{1}[d\text{ leaks}],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> contains pages with at least one in-scope identifier.
We report <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{DocLeak}_{\mathrm{all}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>DocLeak</mi><mi>all</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{DocLeak}_{\mathrm{all}}</annotation></semantics></math> over all PII and
<math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{DocLeak}_{\mathrm{crit}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>DocLeak</mi><mi>crit</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{DocLeak}_{\mathrm{crit}}</annotation></semantics></math> over Direct and Linkage identifiers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Headline DocLeak uses type-aware matching. The error analyses additionally
use type-agnostic matching to measure whether an identifier would be
spatially masked despite an incorrect type. DocLeak penalizes unmatched gold instances but does not penalize extra predictions. We therefore report it jointly with F1<sub id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">loc</span></sub> and F1<sub id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">type</span></sub>, whose precision terms count unmatched predictions as false positives. One-to-one IoU matching prevents a single prediction from receiving credit for
multiple gold instances.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Dataset: Collection and Composition</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Sources and generation process</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LeakageBench</span> contains <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">500</span> document-page images sampled from public operational-style business documents. We position the dataset as a challenge set for stress-testing image-based PII redaction under heterogeneous layouts, dense tables, scanned correspondence, mixed acquisition channels, and visual degradation. Rather than claiming to represent all deployment settings, LeakageBench covers a focused slice of business-document redaction workflows where identifiers appear across forms, invoices, emails, letters, and free-form correspondence.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Source A: OCR-IDL (public archive documents).</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We sample <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">103</span> documents (113) pages from OCR-IDL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Biten et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, which provides standardized OCR outputs for documents from the UCSF Industry Documents Library (IDL) <span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                
                
                
              <a href="https://industrydocuments.ucsf.edu/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://industrydocuments.ucsf.edu/</a></span></span></span>, a large digital archive of industry documents hosted by UCSF.
OCR-IDL is valuable for our setting because it includes heterogeneous, historically scanned/archived pages with substantial layout and rendering variation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Source B: VRDU Ad-Buy Forms (structured, table-heavy invoices/receipts).</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We sample <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">107</span> documents (222) pages from the VRDU Ad-buy Forms corpus released by Google Research <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
These documents are public Federal Communications Commission (FCC) <span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
                
                
                
              <a href="https://publicfiles.fcc.gov/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://publicfiles.fcc.gov/</a></span></span></span> filings and are dominated by structured invoices/receipts with multi-column layouts and repeated/nested table structures, providing a concentrated stress-test for localization within dense tabular regions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Source C: Unstructured operational-style documents (free-form correspondence).</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We sample the remaining <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">81</span> documents (165) pages from FCC public filings, selecting free-form pages that resemble internal operational documents: email threads and attachments, letters and memos, scanned correspondence, and mixed-format “file” pages.
Compared to invoice- or form-heavy sources, these pages exhibit less templated structure and place identifiers in narrative body text, signatures, headers/footers, and embedded attachments.
This source therefore stresses redaction systems under realistic cross-field co-reference (the same individual referenced across multiple regions) and non-field PII placement.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Identifiability-first scope</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Privacy regulation is triggered by <em id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">identifiability</em>, not by whether a string resembles a name.
Under the GDPR, personal data includes identifiers such as names, identification numbers, and location data (Art. 4(1)) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">European Union, 2016</a>)</cite>.
Recital 26 emphasizes that identifiability must consider <em id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">all means reasonably likely to be used</em>, including <em id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">singling out</em> and linkage by other parties <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">European Union, 2016</a>)</cite>.
Similarly, the CPRA/CCPA defines personal information as data that could reasonably be linked (directly or indirectly) to a consumer or household <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">California Legislature, 2025</a>)</cite>,
and explicitly recognizes that personal information can exist in physical formats, including paper documents and printed images <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">California Legislature, 2025</a>)</cite>.
In U.S. standards, PII is likewise defined to include information that is <em id="S4.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">linked or linkable</em> to an individual <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2010</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Consequently, a redaction benchmark must treat as in-scope not only direct identifiers, such as names and contacts, but also <em id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">linkage keys</em>
(policy numbers, case IDs, customer IDs) that resolve to a person through common workflows.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>PII schema: re-identification surfaces</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We annotate fine-grained labels for auditing, but report results using three privacy-aligned groups that reflect how identifiability arises in operational document workflows: (i) direct identification, (ii) lookup/linkage, and (iii) contextual inference.
Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.3 PII schema: re-identification surfaces ‣ 4 Dataset: Collection and Composition ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes the grouping used for reporting and analysis and lists the fine-grained labels covered under each group.</p>
</div>

<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Rationale.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Direct identifiers</span> explicitly reveal identity or contact information <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">European Union, 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">California Legislature, 2025</a>)</cite>.
<span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Linkage keys</span> identify via lookup: they may appear innocuous on the page but act as stable keys into organizational systems or registries, consistent with standards that treat unique identifying numbers and codes as identifying <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2010</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2025</a>)</cite> and with CPRA/CCPA “unique identifiers” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">California Legislature, 2025</a>)</cite>.
Finally, we annotate <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">contextual identifiers</span> (e.g., dates and entity fields) because they increase identifiability through co-occurrence and linkage in real documents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">European Union, 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2010</a>)</cite>.
We do not assume each contextual field is personal data in isolation; rather, it captures <em id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">re-identification surfaces</em> that amplify risk when combined with direct identifiers or linkage keys.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Dataset statistics and diagnostic views</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Spatial PII heatmap. ‣ 4.4 Dataset statistics and diagnostic views ‣ 4 Dataset: Collection and Composition ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> reports composition and label volume for <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LeakageBench</span> (released) and for each source, including document and page counts and PII group totals.
Redaction safety is determined by document-level worst cases. We therefore provide diagnostic views that expose the benchmark’s risk profile: (i) the identifiers-per-page distribution (Fig. <a href="#S4.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Spatial PII heatmap. ‣ 4.4 Dataset statistics and diagnostic views ‣ 4 Dataset: Collection and Composition ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) and (ii) the spatial concentration of PII on the page (Fig. <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Spatial PII heatmap. ‣ 4.4 Dataset statistics and diagnostic views ‣ 4 Dataset: Collection and Composition ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Identifiers-per-page distribution.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Spatial PII heatmap. ‣ 4.4 Dataset statistics and diagnostic views ‣ 4 Dataset: Collection and Composition ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows the distribution of PII instances per page.
This distribution is critical for safety: a page leaks if any identifier is missed, so pages with many identifiers place disproportionate pressure on redaction systems.
Across the collected pool, we annotate <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">11,954</span> PII instances over <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">500</span> pages (<span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">23.90</span> per page on average), including <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">4,315</span> critical identifiers from the Direct and Linkage categories (<span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">8.63</span> per page on average).
We therefore report document-level leakage alongside entity-level scores (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Metrics ‣ 3 Task and Evaluation Protocol ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Spatial PII heatmap.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Spatial PII heatmap. ‣ 4.4 Dataset statistics and diagnostic views ‣ 4 Dataset: Collection and Composition ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> visualizes where identifiers appear on the page.
We partition each image into a regular grid of non-overlapping 14×14-pixel patches (stride = 14), yielding 3,600 patches per page (60 × 60).
For each patch, we record which PII categories overlap its area and aggregate the results across all pages.
The resulting heatmap distinguishes benchmarks where PII concentrates in predictable regions-such as headers or signatures-from those where it is distributed throughout tables and body text.
We report both an “all PII” heatmap and a “critical PII” heatmap restricted to Direct+Linkage identifiers.</p>
</div>

<td id="S4.T2.2.2.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:0.6pt;padding-bottom:0.6pt;">11.08</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T2.2.3" class="ltx_tr">

</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Document types.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LeakageBench is dominated by operational business documents: invoices, emails, forms, letters/correspondence, and file-like pages.
Full page-type composition by source is reported in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Document-Type Composition ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Annotation procedure</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All annotations were produced by the first two authors. The 500 page images were randomly split equally and annotated independently following the guidelines in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Annotation Instructions ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>. Annotators labeled entity instances using tight bounding boxes around visible PII spans and transcribed <span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">value</span> strings verbatim (no normalization); multi-line items use the delimiter “<span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">\n</span>”. We annotate fine-grained entity types and additionally report privacy-aligned group aggregates (Direct/Linkage/Contextual) for analysis.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.6 </span>Annotation quality control</h3>

<div id="S4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To assess annotation consistency, each annotator contributed a 10% stratified sample of their assigned pages for cross-annotation by the other annotator (<span id="S4.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">50 images / pages total</span>). Disagreements were resolved by joint adjudication to form a single gold set.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Inter-annotator agreement is measured with Cohen’s <math id="S4.SS6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> over entity instances after alignment.
We align annotations via one-to-one bipartite matching using IoU <math id="S4.SS6.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≥</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq\tau</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S4.SS6.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau{=}0.75" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau{=}0.75</annotation></semantics></math>.
A matched pair is counted as agreement only if both boxes share the same fine-grained type; spatial overlaps with a type mismatch are counted as disagreements.
Any annotation with no IoU<math id="S4.SS6.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq 0.75" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≥</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq 0.75</annotation></semantics></math> counterpart from the other annotator is treated as a miss (disagreement).
Under this protocol, we obtain <math id="S4.SS6.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa=0.979" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.979</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa=0.979</annotation></semantics></math> on the cross-annotated subset.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experimental Setup</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate off-the-shelf systems under one unified image-level redaction protocol.
The baselines cover two architectures.
First, <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OCR-dependent systems</span> read the page with OCR, detect PII in the recognized text, and project detections back to image coordinates using OCR word boxes.
Within this family, we compare a generic redaction pipeline against stronger commercial and task-adapted privacy detectors.
Second, <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OCR-free vision-language models</span> receive the page image directly and predict PII regions without an explicit OCR stage.
All systems are converted to the same prediction format (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Prediction format ‣ 3 Task and Evaluation Protocol ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>) and evaluated with entity-level localization, localization+typing, document-level leakage, schema coverage, and supported-type leakage (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Metrics ‣ 3 Task and Evaluation Protocol ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>).
No system is trained or tuned on LeakageBench.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>OCR-dependent baselines</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All OCR-dependent baselines use the same image-to-box pipeline: OCR extracts text and word-level boxes, a privacy detector predicts typed PII spans over the OCR text, and each span is mapped back to the page by merging the corresponding word boxes.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Generic OCR-dependent redaction.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use Microsoft Presidio Image Redactor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Microsoft (2026)</a></cite> as the generic OCR-dependent baseline.
Presidio applies OCR, detects PII spans with Presidio Analyzer, and returns image-space redaction boxes through OCR word alignment.
We use Tesseract <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Smith (2007)</a></cite> for this baseline and map Presidio entity types to the LeakageBench schema with a fixed mapping.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Commercial and task-adapted OCR-dependent detectors.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate stronger privacy-oriented detectors on top of Amazon Textract OCR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amazon Web Services (2026b)</a></cite>: GLiNER-base <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zaratiana et al. (2024)</a></cite>, Presidio-best (GLiNER restricted), GLiNER multi-PII <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zaratiana (2024)</a></cite>, NVIDIA GLiNER PII <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">NVIDIA (2025)</a></cite>, GLiNER2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zaratiana et al. (2025)</a></cite>, Google DLP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google Cloud (2026)</a></cite>, Amazon Comprehend PII <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amazon Web Services (2026a)</a></cite> and an OpenAI Privacy Filter <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI (2026)</a></cite> pipeline.
These systems test whether stronger text-side PII detectors are sufficient once document-image constraints—OCR errors, dense layouts, repeated identifiers, span fragmentation, and box reconstruction—are introduced.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Schema alignment.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All OCR-dependent systems are scored against the LeakageBench schema.
Unsupported entity types count as missed detections under full-schema evaluation.
We therefore report schema coverage and supported-type leakage to separate taxonomy limitations from empirical detection and localization failures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Baseline Reproducibility Details ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> summarizes the OCR engines, detector settings, schema mappings, and conversion rules for each OCR-dependent baseline.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>OCR-free vision-language baselines</h3>

<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">OCR-free vision-language localization.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate <span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Qwen3-VL-32B</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al. (2025)</a></cite> and <span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">InternVL3-38B</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al. (2025)</a></cite> as OCR-free vision-language baselines because they support explicit 2D grounding from image input.
Unlike OCR-dependent systems, these models receive the page image directly and are prompted to return PII types, values, confidence scores, and bounding boxes.
Predicted boxes are converted to image coordinates and evaluated under the same localization-and-typing protocol as all other systems.
Coordinate conventions and parsing rules are summarized in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Baseline Reproducibility Details ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>; full prompt templates are provided in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Prompt Templates ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Closed OCR-free models.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We additionally evaluate GPT-5.4 using single-pass vision and GPT-5.5 in two
configurations: single-pass vision and Code Interpreter-assisted inspection.
All configurations use the same PII taxonomy and semantic instructions and
return structured predictions with integer bounding boxes in a normalized
<math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="999" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>999</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">999</annotation></semantics></math> coordinate system. For GPT-5.5, we use high image detail and medium
reasoning effort; in the tool-assisted configuration, Code Interpreter is
required to inspect the page and may crop or zoom regions before returning the
final prediction. All outputs are processed using the same parsing, coordinate
conversion, and evaluation pipeline as the other OCR-free models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Prompt-driven schema coverage.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For OCR-free systems, the full LeakageBench schema is supplied in the prompt.
Their schema coverage is therefore <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0</annotation></semantics></math> by configuration: the model is allowed to emit every benchmark type, but this does not imply reliable detection.
Empirical failures are captured by entity-level F1, document-level leakage, group leakage, and output-validity rates.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Why not LayoutLM-style trained baselines.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LeakageBench is evaluated as an off-the-shelf challenge set: systems must run without training on the benchmark and must return PII types with image-space boxes. LayoutLM-style document NER models typically require supervised fine-tuning, task-specific heads, OCR-token alignment, and a train/dev/test split. We therefore leave layout-aware trained models to a future trained-baseline track.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Results</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S6.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 6 Results ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reports full-schema performance at IoU <math id="S6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.75" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.75</annotation></semantics></math> under the unified prediction format. To assess sensitivity to box tightness, Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G IoU Threshold Sweep ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a> reports results at <math id="S6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\in\{0.50,0.75,0.95\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0.50</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.75</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.95</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\in\{0.50,0.75,0.95\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We report localization F1, localization+typing F1, document-level leakage over all identifiers, and leakage over safety-critical Direct+Linkage identifiers.
Unless stated otherwise, unsupported schema types, invalid outputs, and out-of-bounds boxes are counted as missed detections.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For systems with restricted taxonomies, we additionally report supported-type leakage in Table <a href="#S6.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 6 Results ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, where gold labels are filtered to the entity types each system can emit.
Schema coverage and full-schema group-wise leakage are reported in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Schema Coverage ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a> and Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Group-Level Leakage ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>.
Valid denotes the fraction of pages producing parseable, schema-conformant outputs. Malformed or unusable outputs are scored as empty prediction sets; individual invalid boxes are rejected and receive no credit.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.T3" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S6.T3.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S6.T3.2.1" class="ltx_tr">

Full-schema results on <span id="S6.T3.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LeakageBench</span> at IoU <math id="S6.T3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.75" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.75</annotation></semantics></math>.
Textract systems share identical OCR, isolating detector differences.
F1<sub id="S6.T3.9" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S6.T3.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">loc</span></sub> is page-macro type-agnostic localization F1;
F1<sub id="S6.T3.10" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S6.T3.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">type</span></sub> also requires the correct type.
DocLeak<sub id="S6.T3.11" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S6.T3.11.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">all</span></sub> and DocLeak<sub id="S6.T3.12" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S6.T3.12.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">crit</span></sub> are the fractions of pages leaking any identifier and any Direct+Linkage identifier, respectively. Unsupported types and invalid outputs count as misses; Table <a href="#S6.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 6 Results ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> controls for schema coverage. Valid denotes parseable, schema-conformant page outputs. Bold marks the best result, including ties.
</figcaption>
</figure>

Supported-schema leakage at IoU <math id="S6.T4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.75" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.75</annotation></semantics></math>.
Coverage is the fraction of benchmark types supported; Unsup. pages
contain at least one unsupported gold type.
Group scores retain only supported gold types.
The full-schema Textract block fixes OCR and schema, isolating the
detector.
Bold marks the best coverage within the restricted-schema block and the
lowest leakage within each full-schema block.
Restricted-schema leakage is not ranked because supported type sets
differ.

<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Analysis</h3>

<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Overall safety picture.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S6.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 6 Results ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows that stronger systems improve
entity-level localization without achieving document-level safety.
Amazon Comprehend PII obtains the highest localization F1
(F1<math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{}_{\mathrm{loc}}=0.304" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>loc</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.304</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\mathrm{loc}}=0.304</annotation></semantics></math>), while GPT-5.5 with Code Interpreter
obtains the highest typed F1 (F1<math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{}_{\mathrm{type}}=0.119" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>type</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.119</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\mathrm{type}}=0.119</annotation></semantics></math>).
Nevertheless, both have DocLeak<math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{}_{\mathrm{crit}}=0.968" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>crit</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.968</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\mathrm{crit}}=0.968</annotation></semantics></math>, showing
that better average detection does not guarantee that a page is safe
to release.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This conclusion is robust to the matching scope. Crediting any
IoU-eligible box regardless of its predicted type reduces the
DocLeak<sub id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">crit</span></sub> range from 0.968–1.000 under headline
type-aware matching to 0.945–1.000 under type-agnostic matching.
Thus, the high leakage rates are not primarily caused by type-label
errors.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Leakage is severe, not marginal.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To complement binary DocLeak, we count unmatched critical identifiers per
page. Across systems, leaking pages retain <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5.3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.3</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8.7</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8.7</annotation></semantics></math> critical identifiers
on average. Even the lowest-severity system misses <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5.3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.3</annotation></semantics></math> per leaking page
(median <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>; P90 <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="11" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>11</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">11</annotation></semantics></math>), corresponding to approximately <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="66\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>66</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">66\%</annotation></semantics></math> of critical
identifiers across applicable pages. Thus, leakage typically reflects multiple
exposed identifiers rather than an isolated miss. Complete per-system severity statistics are reported in Table <a href="#A9.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ Appendix I Additional Error Diagnostics ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Schema coverage is not enough.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Schema coverage diagnostics are reported in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Schema Coverage ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>.
Restricted systems such as Presidio, Presidio-best (GLiNER restricted), and Amazon Comprehend PII cover only 20.8% of benchmark types, while Google DLP and the OpenAI Privacy Filter cover 25.0%.
These restricted systems cover Direct identifiers but miss most Linkage keys under our schema mapping, making lookup-style identifiers a persistent coverage gap.
However, full label coverage does not solve the task either: GLiNER-base, GLiNER multi-PII, and NVIDIA GLiNER PII are configured with full schema coverage, yet their Linkage leakage remains near-total in Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Group-Level Leakage ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>.
This suggests that sparse lookup keys, dense tables, OCR fragmentation, and layout variation remain difficult even when the label set is available.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Supported-schema leakage isolates detection failures.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S6.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 6 Results ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> filters gold labels to the types each system can emit and reports leakage by privacy group.
Even under this easier setting, leakage remains high: full-schema OCR-dependent systems still leak on more than 94% of Direct pages and more than 96% of Linkage pages.
This shows that failures are not only taxonomy mismatches; OCR errors, repeated identifiers, span fragmentation, and box reconstruction also contribute to residual exposure.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">OCR-dependent failure attribution.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Full results appear in Appendix Tables <a href="#A9.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ Appendix I Additional Error Diagnostics ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>–<a href="#A9.T15" title="Table 15 ‣ Appendix I Additional Error Diagnostics ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>. Using type-agnostic matching, we attribute each leaked critical identifier to an OCR miss, a detector miss with zero box overlap, or a box/alignment failure with positive overlap below <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.75" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.75</annotation></semantics></math>; one-to-one assignment conflicts account for at most <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.2\%</annotation></semantics></math>. Box/alignment failure is the largest category for seven of nine OCR-dependent systems, accounting for <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="45.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>45.9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">45.9</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="84.5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>84.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">84.5\%</annotation></semantics></math> of their attributable leaks, while detector misses vary from <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>15.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15.5</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="48.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>48.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">48.8\%</annotation></semantics></math>. Independently of any detector, Textract cannot recover 623/4,280 value-bearing critical annotations (<math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="14.6\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>14.6</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">14.6\%</annotation></semantics></math>), compared with 765/4,280 (<math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="17.9\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>17.9</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">17.9\%</annotation></semantics></math>) for Tesseract. Performance differences among the Textract-based pipelines therefore arise primarily downstream of their shared OCR stage.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.T5" class="ltx_table">

<td id="S6.T5.2.6.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">98.9</td>
<td id="S6.T5.2.6.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">0.2</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>
Error attribution for leaked Direct and Linkage identifiers from OCR-free
VLMs at <math id="S6.T5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{IoU}=0.75" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>IoU</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{IoU}=0.75</annotation></semantics></math>, using type-agnostic matching.
Attribution columns are percentages of the leaked critical instances shown
in the second numeric column and sum to 100%.
Interface denotes identifiers on pages without a fully valid output;
Zero-IoU denotes no overlapping prediction; Box fail denotes positive
overlap below the IoU threshold; and Assignment denotes one-to-one
matching conflicts.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Formatting versus localization in OCR-free VLMs.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S6.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ OCR-dependent failure attribution. ‣ 6.1 Analysis ‣ 6 Results ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> separates interface failures from
failures on valid outputs using a common denominator of leaked critical
identifiers. Interface failures account for 27.8% and 36.9% of
leakage for Qwen3-VL-32B and InternVL3-38B, respectively, but none for
GPT-5.4 or either GPT-5.5 configuration. Among residual leaked critical
instances, sub-threshold boxes account for 51.7% for Qwen3-VL-32B,
83.5% for GPT-5.4, 96.1% for GPT-5.5, and 98.9% for GPT-5.5 with
Code Interpreter. These percentages describe the composition of the
errors that remain, not the overall localization-failure rate. A larger
box-failure share can therefore coexist with improved
F1<sub id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">loc</span></sub> when total leakage decreases and zero-overlap
misses decline more sharply. InternVL3-38B instead exhibits a larger
share of zero-overlap misses (35.1%). Thus, interface reliability is
necessary but insufficient; spatial localization remains the dominant
limitation for the GPT configurations and Qwen3-VL-32B.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2609.02207v1/qualitative_errors.png" id="S6.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/263;" width="476" height="263" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Representative failure modes. Panels (a)–(c) use
GLiNER-multi-PII with Textract; panel (d) compares GPT-5.5
single-pass and tool-assisted localization. Green denotes gold
boxes, orange dashed boxes sub-threshold predictions, blue
tool-assisted predictions, and magenta dotted boxes OCR regions.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Tool assistance improves OCR-free localization, but leakage remains high.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S6.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Formatting versus localization in OCR-free VLMs. ‣ 6.1 Analysis ‣ 6 Results ‣ LeakageBench: Document-Level Leakage Risk for Redacting Personally Identifiable Information in Document Images" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> illustrates these failures and a
tool-assisted localization correction. Within GPT-5.5, Code
Interpreter raises F1<sub id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px7.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">loc</span></sub> from 0.090 to 0.249 and
F1<sub id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px7.p1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">type</span></sub> from 0.050 to 0.119. It reduces
DocLeak<sub id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px7.p1.1.3" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px7.p1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">crit</span></sub> from 0.990 to 0.968 and reduces Direct and
Contextual leakage from 0.956 to 0.887 and from 0.986 to 0.908,
respectively. Linkage leakage nevertheless remains 0.964.
Tool-assisted inspection therefore improves spatial grounding
substantially, but does not yet provide release-level redaction safety.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px8" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Takeaway.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LeakageBench is best viewed as a redaction-safety challenge set rather
than a leaderboard where systems differ only by small margins. The
benchmark exposes complementary failure modes: restricted taxonomies
omit identifier groups, OCR-dependent pipelines propagate recognition
and alignment errors, and OCR-free VLMs remain limited by spatial
grounding. Code Interpreter substantially improves GPT-5.5
localization, but the resulting system still leaks critical PII on
96.8% of applicable pages. These findings motivate systems that
combine broad schema coverage, robust visual reading, and tight,
high-recall localization.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Ethical, Legal, and Release Protocol</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LeakageBench is intended for defensive research on document-redaction
safety. Although the source documents originate from public
collections, combining real document images with fine-grained PII
annotations introduces privacy and dual-use risks. The document images
and annotations will therefore be made available for research use under
a privacy- and license-aware Data Use Agreement (DUA).</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The benchmark is intended for evaluating privacy-preserving redaction,
not for re-identification or PII mining. Its GDPR-aligned schema
supports comparative evaluation but does not define legal compliance
or prescribe which fields must be redacted in every jurisdiction or
deployment setting.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Limitations</h2>

<div id="Sx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LeakageBench is a 500-page challenge set drawn from public business
documents, not a representative sample of all redaction settings. It
does not cover heavily handwritten, medical, legal-discovery,
multilingual, or non-U.S. documents. Evaluation is page-local and
does not measure multi-page contextual inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The schema follows an identifiability-first view. Direct identifiers
and Linkage keys are primary release-safety targets, whereas masking
Contextual identifiers depends on the applicable policy.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Headline DocLeak uses conservative type-aware matching at IoU
<math id="Sx2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.75" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.75</annotation></semantics></math>, so a wrongly typed but correctly localized box counts as
a leak. However, type-agnostic matching yields the same substantive
conclusion, with DocLeak<sub id="Sx2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_sub"><span id="Sx2.p3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">crit</span></sub> remaining between 0.945
and 1.000. Axis-aligned boxes and IoU do not directly measure pixel
coverage of skewed, handwritten, or irregular regions. Although F1
penalizes extra predictions, we do not define a document-level
over-redaction or utility metric.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Error attribution is limited by the stored artifacts: 35 critical
annotations lack usable verbatim values, span-level alignment logs
are unavailable, and Google DLP’s vendor OCR is not stored.
Consequently, box and alignment errors cannot be separated fully.
The OCR-free results also represent specific model and inference
configurations whose API behavior may change.</p>
</div>
</section>

<li id="bib.bib29" class="ltx_bibitem ltx_bib_misc"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_bib_author-year ltx_role_refnum ltx_tag_bibitem">Google Cloud (2026)</span>
